approved: Criticised the government for still not having a permanent Military Justice bill four years after the High Court's 2009 Lane v Morrison decision struck down the Australian Military Court, noting Minister Faulkner had called fixing military justice the government's highest priority yet only interim measures bills have followed.

Supported the bill as a RAAF reserve legal officer himself, explained the Australian Military Court was established in 2006 with a chief military judge, two permanent judges and a reserve panel before being struck down in the Lane and Morrison case, and praised ADF personnel operating in extreme conditions such as 51 degree heat in Afghanistan.

Explained the interim measures extend judicial tenure by two years pending a permanent Military Court, noted the Howard government implemented 32 of 40 recommendations when establishing the Australian Military Court in 2007, and said Labor's more than $25 billion in defence cuts have left the defence industry workforce at just 24,000 to 25,000 jobs, far below the 34,000 predicted for 2013.

Summed up the bill, confirming it extends the tenure of the Chief Judge Advocate and judge advocate's panel by a further two years beyond their September expiry, and rejected opposition criticism by pointing to increased defence spending in this year's budget.

The Military Justice (Interim Measures) Amendment Bill 2013 extends the tenure of the Chief Judge Advocate and other statutory office holders by two years, supported by the coalition to maintain the status quo while a permanent military court is developed. The speaker urged parliament not to delay, stressing the need for surety and clear processes for ADF personnel, especially those in combat zones.
